chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
title: Bix Beiderbecke versus Red Nichols
summary: They discuss why Trumbauer's solo stuck in people's minds and why Bix was idolised over Red Nichols, though Dickenson hears only similarity.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: One of the things that always seemed odd to me also is... You know, in talking about "Singing The Blues," it's Trumbauer's solo that really seemed to stick in people's mind, and not so much Bix. And...
No, it wasn't. It wasn't as much Bix as it was Trumbauer.

And of course, the critics and practically everything you read, Bix is put in a much higher position than Red Nichols. Usually they say Red Nichols was just a Bix imitator, and then they put him in a...
But yet, you mentioned Red Nichols, and Roy mentioned him and so on. So it seems that he may have been more famous than Bix at that time, and he certainly made more records.
The only thing that was an advantage with Bix was that Bix played piano, too. You know what I mean? He made his famous number, 'In A Mist.'
So Bix was looked at as more...

They played similar, but not the same. But they played much similar to each other. I don't think Red Nichols copied Bix. I think it just was a similarity in their playing. Like, there was a similarity in Red Allen and Louis; there was a similarity in their playing. But I don't think one was...one could have had an influence on the other. But the only one that would have it would be Armstrong would have had an influence on Red...
On Red. Sure. Well, Red was seven years younger.
Yeah. But on the whole, they didn't play exactly the same thing. It sounded on the same order and
